descriptions: The movement shares a question rather than an ultimate: what is the visible fruit of the homeless life, and is there fruit of deeds and another world? Each teacher answers differently (DN 2).
negations: Several of its teachers deny any fruit of deeds or any other world (DN 2: Pūraṇa, Ajita).
relation_to_self: Contested within the movement: an eternal jīva among seven bodies (Pakudha), a person made of four elements that is annihilated (Ajita), no statement at all (Sañjaya).
relation_to_world: Contested: fixed by niyati (Gosāla), eternal and barren (Pakudha), simply ends at death (Ajita).
caveat: The śramaṇa movement is not one school: it includes Jains and Buddhists (who have their own views, U34–U36) and teachers who deny any ultimate. A one-truth reading would have to override the explicit denials of Pūraṇa and Ajita and the refusal of Sañjaya.

names.name: the end of suffering after the fixed round (dukkhass' anta)

descriptions: (As reported) All beings are transformed by niyati, saṅgati and bhāva (DN 2).
(As reported) Pleasure and pain are measured out as with a measure; saṃsāra has fixed limits (DN 2).
(Tamil report) The lord is the boundless knower who pervades endless things everywhere and always; release is reached in the supreme white birth (Maṇimēkalai 27.108–165).
negations: No cause or condition for the defilement or purification of beings (DN 2).
No exertion, strength, energy or human effort (Uvāsagadasāo 7).
relation_to_self: (As reported) The jīva is real and transmigrates through the fixed round; in the Jain account a soul can re-enter successive bodies (reanimation).
relation_to_world: (As reported) The world-course is fixed in every detail and runs through 8,400,000 great aeons for every being.
caveat: No Ājīvika text survives; every statement comes from hostile Buddhist, Jain or Tamil sources. Niyati is a governing order, not a ground of being, and the sources never present it as 'the one truth'. The Tamil report of a 'lord who is the boundless knower' may refer to the omniscient teacher rather than a creator; it is recorded as the source gives it.

names.name: the four elements (bhūta-catuṣṭaya) as the only principles
the world as far as the senses reach (yāvān indriyagocaraḥ)

descriptions: (As reported) 'Earth, water, fire, air: these are the principles' (Bṛhaspati Sūtra fragment).
(As reported) The variety of the world — fire hot, water cold, wind temperate — is fixed by svabhāva, not by an unseen cause (Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha 1).
negations: No other world, no self that goes to it (paralokino 'bhāvāt paralokābhāvaḥ).
No heaven or liberation other than pleasure and the death of the body; no lord but the king.
(Jayarāśi) Not even the elements 'stand when examined' — no principle is established.
relation_to_self: (As reported) The self is the living body qualified by consciousness; it ends with the body.
relation_to_world: (As reported) The world is the perceptible aggregate of four elements.
caveat: The Cārvāka denies any ultimate beyond what perception shows and explicitly denies another world, an unseen cause and liberation; Jayarāśi denies that any principle can be established. Any one-truth reading runs against these denials; the school would call it the priests' 'livelihood'.

descriptions: (As reported) To every question about the other world, spontaneously born beings, fruit of deeds and the Tathāgata after death, in all four forms, the answer is refused (DN 2).
negations: 'I do not say it is so, nor thus, nor otherwise, nor not so, nor not not so.'
relation_to_self: Not asserted: (Jain report) 'who knows whether the soul exists, and what use is knowing it?'
caveat: The Ajñānikas refuse to affirm any ultimate; to read their refusal as pointing to an ineffable one truth would be an interpretation they are reported to reject as another assertion. Both Buddhist and Jain reporters insist their own undeclared points and 'inexpressible' (avaktavya) differ from this refusal.
